chapter.name: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science

questions.q: Aarav wants to model one question only: will a ball hit for a six clear the boundary without touching the ground first? Which set of details should his simple model keep?
questions.a: The mass of the ball and the speed and direction in which it is hit
o: The mass of the ball and the speed and direction in which it is hit
The brand of the bat, the colour of the ball and the amount of grass on the field
The stitching of the seam, the spin of the ball and the air resistance it meets
The colour of the ball, the speed it is hit at and the brand of the bat

questions.q: A coach's simple model of sixes is right on most shots but misses by a few metres on heavily spun shots. What does the chapter suggest as the sensible next step?
questions.a: Add smaller effects such as spin to the model, for greater accuracy
o: Add smaller effects such as spin to the model, for greater accuracy
Throw the model out, since any model that ignored a detail was a mistake
Remove speed and direction, since the missed shots prove they do not matter
Stop modelling, since real shots cannot be captured by simple models

questions.q: A Class 9 group must explain how the heart pumps blood to the whole body. Which model suits that question best?
questions.a: One that ignores single cells and treats the heart as a working system
o: One that ignores single cells and treats the heart as a working system
One that draws every single cell of the heart wall along with each of its parts
One that treats the heart as a single point, as a car is treated in physics
One that treats the heart as a hot gas, as Saha treated the matter in a star

questions.q: Neha models a stone dropped from a balcony and neglects air resistance. Her friend says, 'Air is there, so your model is wrong.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The omission is deliberate; it lets her see the basic effect of gravity alone
o: The omission is deliberate; it lets her see the basic effect of gravity alone
You are right, because leaving a detail out is always an error in building a model
You are right, because a model must contain every detail that really exists
You are wrong, because air has been shown to have no effect on a falling stone

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the field and the way the chapter says that field simplifies a real system (column II).
Column I: 1. A chart shows a water molecule as three balls joined by two sticks  2. A speed calculation treats a bus as a dot moving along a road  3. A sketch of a leaf cell labels only the parts needed to explain one process  4. A planet is drawn as a smooth ball cut into distinct regions
Column II: a. Biology: a cell shown as a diagram highlighting key parts  b. Chemistry: atoms and molecules as spheres and bonds  c. Earth science: a smooth sphere layered into regions  d. Physics: a moving object as a single point
questions.a: The molecule drawn with balls and sticks is chemistry, the bus as a dot is physics, the leaf-cell sketch is biology and the layered planet is earth science.

questions.q:
Read these statements about models.
Statement 1: Neglecting air resistance in a falling-object model is a mistake that the scientist must correct at once.
Statement 2: Saha's model of a star kept temperature, pressure and the way atoms formed ions.
Statement 3: In a model of a six, the brand of the bat matters as much as the mass of the ball.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is correct. Neglecting air resistance is a deliberate choice, and the brand of the bat makes no difference to whether the ball clears the boundary, unlike the mass of the ball.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A model of the heart that ignores individual cells can still explain how the organ pumps blood.
Reason (R): A model is built by choosing the details that answer the question and ignoring those that do not.
questions.a: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: the cells are ignored on purpose so the heart can be understood as a working system.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A student models her cycle ride home using only the distance and her average speed. Her model predicts the ___ the ride will take.
questions.a: time

questions.q: Which statement about ignoring details in a model is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says these choices are not mistakes; they are made on purpose. So the statement calling them slips is the one it does not support.
o: The ignored details are slips that a careful scientist hopes nobody notices
The ignored details are chosen on purpose to keep the model simple enough
More details can be added as a model grows more complex, for greater accuracy
The ignored details are those that make little difference to the question asked

questions.q: True or False? A scientist who leaves the spin of a cricket ball out of a simple model of a six has made a mistake. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Spin is one of the smaller effects that can be ignored in a simple model, and leaving it out is a deliberate choice; it can be added later if more accuracy is wanted.

questions.q:
Priya rides 3 km from school to home at an average speed of 12 km/h.
(a) Using only these two quantities, how many minutes does her model predict for the ride?
(b) Her model ignores the colour of her bicycle. Why does this not change the prediction?
questions.a: (a) 3 km at 12 km/h is 3/12 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes. (b) The colour changes neither the distance nor the speed, so it cannot change the time.
s: Part (b): colour affects neither distance nor speed

questions.q:
Saha's model of a star left many things out.
(a) Name two kinds of detail inside a star that he chose not to model.
(b) Using your answer, say what the model gained by leaving them out.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: the behaviour of every atom, every reaction, every movement inside the star. (b) It could focus on temperature, pressure and the way atoms formed ions, which explained how a star's colour is connected to its temperature.
s: Part (b): focus gained and the explanation it gave

questions.q: A physicist studies a car on a road and a biologist studies the heart. Compare the simplification each makes, saying what is ignored or reduced.
questions.a: The physicist may reduce the car to a single point, while the biologist ignores many individual cells so that the heart is seen as a functioning system. Both keep only what the question needs.
s: Physics: car reduced to a single point
Biology: individual cells ignored, organ seen as a system

questions.q: Write one question about a school-bus journey that a simple model could answer. Name one detail you would keep and one you would ignore.
questions.a: For example: 'How long will the journey take?' Keep the distance and the average speed; ignore the colour of the bus, which does not affect the time.
s: A question a model can answer, with a kept detail
An ignored detail that makes no difference to that question

questions.q: The chapter says that ignoring details is 'not a mistake'. Using the heart as the example, explain what makes it a choice and not a slip.
questions.a: When studying how the heart pumps blood, many individual cells are ignored on purpose so that the organ can be understood as a working system; the aim is to keep things simple enough and still answer the question.
s: Cells ignored on purpose in the heart example
Reason: simple enough but still answers the question

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Our model of the six leaves out air resistance, spin and the seam, so it is wrong.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The chapter lists air resistance, spin and the seam as smaller effects that can be ignored in a simple model, and ignoring them is deliberate. If more accuracy is needed, extra details can be added as the model grows more complex.
s: These are smaller effects, ignored on purpose
Details can be added later for greater accuracy

questions.q: Sam proposes a model of the six that keeps the bat's brand, the colour of the ball and the amount of grass, and ignores the ball's mass, speed and direction. Show that this model cannot answer whether the ball clears the boundary.
questions.a: The boundary question depends on the mass of the ball and the speed and direction of the hit, which Sam ignores. The brand, colour and grass make no difference to it, so his model keeps only what does not matter and could not tell a gentle hit from a powerful one.
s: Names what the question depends on
Shows Sam kept details that make no difference
Concludes the model cannot separate different hits

questions.q: A model keeps only temperature, pressure and the way atoms form ions, and ignores everything else inside the object. Write the question about the sky it was built to answer, name the scientist and say what the model explains.
questions.a: Question: 'Why do stars have different colours?' Meghnad Saha treated the matter in a star as a hot gas and focused on temperature, pressure and ion formation; this explained how a star's colour is deeply connected to its temperature.

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'A good model leaves out the right details; it does not try to include all of them.' Use (i) the cricket six, (ii) the heart and (iii) Saha's star, and say what a model that tried to include everything would fail to do.
questions.a: (i) For the six, mass, speed and direction are kept; bat brand, ball colour and grass are ignored. (ii) For the heart, individual cells are ignored so it is seen as a working system. (iii) Saha ignored every atom, reaction and movement and kept temperature, pressure and ion formation. A model with everything would not be simple enough to let us find the answer to the question; the natural world is too complex to study in full detail.
s: Saha: what he ignored and kept
States the general point about the right details
A model with everything is too complex to answer anything

questions.q:
Riya's home is 4.5 km from school and she cycles at an average speed of 15 km/h.
(i) What time does the simplest model, using only distance and speed, predict?
(ii) A level crossing makes her wait 3 minutes on most days. What does the model predict if this detail is added?
(iii) Is adding the crossing a correction of a mistake? Explain with the chapter's idea.
(iv) Riya must reach by 8:00. Should she include the crossing when planning when to leave?
questions.a: (i) 4.5/15 = 0.3 h = 18 minutes. (ii) 18 + 3 = 21 minutes. (iii) No, the first model left the crossing out on purpose to stay simple; adding a detail gives more accuracy as models grow more complex. (iv) Including it is sensible: the wait happens on most days, so the model that includes it is the better guide; leaving it out would underestimate by 3 minutes.
s: Adding detail is for accuracy, not correcting a mistake

questions.q:
A cricket academy in Nagpur builds software that tells a batter whether a hit will clear a 70 m boundary. The first version uses only the ball's mass (160 g), the speed of the hit and its direction. It ignores the bat's brand, the ball's colour, the grass on the field, the air resistance, the spin and the seam. On 20 recorded shots, the software was right on 17; all 3 wrong answers were heavily spun shots. Adding spin needs a high-speed camera costing Rs 6 lakh and makes each answer take 40 seconds instead of 2.
(a) Which of the ignored items make no difference to the boundary question, and which are only smaller effects?
(b) What does the chapter suggest the academy do about the 3 wrong answers?
(c) What percentage of the shots did the first version get right, and what does that say about its simplification?
(d) The academy can keep the quick model or buy the camera. Choose one and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) Brand, colour and grass make no difference; air resistance, spin and the seam are smaller effects that can be ignored in a simple model. (b) Add the extra detail (spin) for greater accuracy, since models are made more complex when needed. (c) 17/20 = 85%; the simple model already answers most shots, so the simplification was reasonable. (d) Either choice if justified: the quick model keeps answers fast and cheap but misses spun shots; the camera model captures spin but costs Rs 6 lakh and takes 40 s.
s: Part (a): separates no-difference items from smaller effects
Part (b): add the detail for greater accuracy
Part (d): a justified choice with the cost named

questions.q:
Two groups at a school science fair in Vadodara must answer the judges' question: 'How does the heart pump blood around the body?' Group A spends five weeks drawing a model that shows each cell of the heart wall. Group B spends one week building a working pump that moves coloured water around a loop and ignores cells. The judges say a second, deeper question about the heart will be announced only on the day of the fair. The school can send one group.
(a) Which group's model fits the judges' first question, and why?
(b) Name one thing Group B's model cannot tell the viewer.
(c) Group A says 'ignoring the cells is a mistake'. Reply using the chapter.
(d) Which group would you send, given the unknown second question? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Group B: the question is about the heart as a working system, which a model ignoring individual cells shows. (b) How an individual cell of the heart behaves, since cells were ignored. (c) Ignoring details is not a mistake; it is done on purpose to keep the model simple enough to answer the question. (d) Either with a reason: B fits the known question and can add detail later as models grow more complex; A already holds cell-level detail that a deeper question may need.
s: Part (a): Group B and the system reason
Part (b): a cell-level detail it cannot show
Part (c): ignoring is deliberate, not a mistake
Part (d): a justified choice that uses the trade-off

questions.q: A lab in Chennai and a lab in Pune both report the mass of a sample as 2.50 kg. Why can their results be compared directly?
questions.a: Both used the kilogram, a unit based on an agreed international standard
o: Both used the kilogram, a unit based on an agreed international standard
Both kept a local object in their own city as the standard for the kilogram
Both wrote the symbol m, and a symbol alone fixes the amount measured
Both reported the same number, and a number alone fixes the amount

questions.q: A cargo plane needs 4,000 kg of fuel. The fuel's density is 0.80 kg per litre, which is 1.76 lb per litre. A clerk divides 4,000 by 1.76 where 0.80 should have been used. About how many litres short is the plane?
questions.a: Correct litres = 4000/0.80 = 5000. Loaded = 4000/1.76 = about 2273. Shortfall = 5000 - 2273 = about 2727 litres.
o: About 2,727 litres short
About 2,273 litres short
About 1,727 litres short
About 1,000 litres short

questions.q: Shruti hears 'the force of his speech was strong' on television and then reads 'the force on the cart increases' in her science book. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: In science, force has a specific, defined meaning, unlike its loose everyday use
o: In science, force has a specific, defined meaning, unlike its loose everyday use
Force has exactly the same meaning in both and science only adds a symbol F
The scientific meaning of force is looser and more flexible than the everyday one
Science avoids everyday words altogether, so force cannot be a scientific term

questions.q: Arun says the symbol c for the speed of light is a poor choice because it is not a convenient abbreviation. How does the chapter answer him?
questions.a: Symbols often come from history and agreement; c comes from the Latin celeritas, meaning speed
o: Symbols often come from history and agreement; c comes from the Latin celeritas, meaning speed
Symbols must abbreviate the English name, so c stands for the English word 'constant' in physics books
Symbols are picked at random, so any other letter would serve equally well in the same way
Symbols are chosen locally by each country, so Arun may use whatever letter he prefers

questions.q: Which practice would work AGAINST the chapter's reason for a shared system of units?
questions.a: A shared system exists so that results can be compared and built on together; two teams with their own units for one quantity is exactly the mix-up that caused the fuel shortfall.
o: Two teams on one project each choosing their own unit for density
Writing the unit next to the value of every quantity that is measured in a lab
Using SI units everywhere so that no conversions are needed
Basing a kilogram on an agreed international standard

questions.q:
Read these statements about units and symbols.
Statement 1: The speed of light is denoted c because c is the first letter of the English word for light.
Statement 2: A kilogram means the same amount everywhere because it rests on an agreed international standard, not a local object.
Statement 3: In the fuel story, the crew used the fuel's density in pounds per litre where kilograms per litre was needed.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The symbol c comes from the Latin word celeritas, meaning speed, so statement 1 is false.
o: 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
2 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A kilogram of rice or vegetables is expected to mean the same amount everywhere.
Reason (R): The speed of light is defined to be exactly 299792458 m/s.
questions.a: Both are true, but the exact value of the speed of light does not explain why a kilogram means the same everywhere; that rests on agreed international standards.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: In the fuel story, the crew used a density number in pounds per litre where kilograms per litre was needed. Because that number is larger than the correct one, the litres they calculated came out too ___.
questions.a: less

questions.q: True or False? A kilogram of rice means the same amount in every shop because the measurement rests on an agreed standard and not on a local object. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says measurements are based on agreed international standards, not local objects or opinions, which lets results be compared and keeps trade fair.

questions.q:
Light travels at 299792458 m/s.
(a) How far does it travel in 0.5 s, in metres?
(b) A student writes the answer as '149896229' with no unit. Why is that answer incomplete for science?
questions.a: (a) 0.5 x 299792458 = 149,896,229 m. (b) A bare number does not fix the quantity: 149,896,229 could be metres or kilometres, which differ a thousandfold; each quantity is tied to a defined unit.
s: Part (b): a number needs its defined unit

questions.q: In the fuel story, (a) what mix-up caused the shortfall, and (b) what does the chapter say would have avoided it?
questions.a: (a) The ground crew used the density of the fuel in pounds per litre rather than kilograms per litre. (b) Using standard (SI) units everywhere avoids conversions and errors.
s: Part (a): pounds per litre used for kilograms per litre

questions.q: Name one everyday word that the chapter says has a specific scientific meaning, and explain why science fixes such meanings.
questions.a: For example force, work, cell or reaction. Science fixes them because scientific ideas must be communicated clearly and unambiguously, so that scientists across the world can describe observations and compare results.
s: A word from the chapter's list

questions.q: A trader says his old stone weight is fine because his customers trust him. Using the chapter, give one reason why a standard unit is still better.
questions.a: A standard unit based on an international agreement means the same everywhere, allows results to be compared and ensures fairness in daily life and trade, whereas trust in a local object cannot make two traders' kilograms equal.
s: States the value of an agreed standard
Links it to fairness in trade

questions.q: Write one rule for a lab sheet that would prevent a unit mix-up of the kind in the fuel story, and say how the rule works.
questions.a: For example: 'Write the unit beside every number and convert everything to SI units before calculating.' It stops a value in lb per litre being treated as kg per litre.

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'A kilogram means the same everywhere because of an agreed international standard, and the symbol c is likewise just a convenient abbreviation of an English word.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The kilogram part is correct: it rests on an agreed international standard. The c part is wrong: c comes from the Latin word celeritas, meaning speed, and the chapter says scientific symbols often come from history and international agreements, not necessarily abbreviations of convenience.

questions.q: Vikram says, 'The aircraft landed with no casualties, so the unit mix-up was harmless.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The mix-up left the aircraft about 15,000 litres short of fuel mid-flight, so it had to glide to an emergency landing that damaged it. It was luck that no one was hurt; the error was serious.
s: The shortfall of about 15,000 litres and glide landing
Damage shows the error was not harmless

questions.q: A report says a plane carried '22,300' of fuel, without saying whether in kg or lb. Taking 1 kg as about 2.2 lb, show that the two readings cannot be treated as the same amount.
questions.a: 22,300 kg is 22,300 kg. But 22,300 lb is 22,300 / 2.2 = about 10,136 kg, which is about 12,164 kg less. So the bare number does not fix the amount.
s: Finds the difference of about 12,164 kg
Concludes the unit must be stated

questions.q: Write a situation from daily life where the lack of a standard measure would cause confusion or unfairness, and say what the chapter's idea of a standard fixes.
questions.a: For example: two cloth sellers each using their own 'metre' stick so that a buyer pays the same price for different lengths. A standard based on an agreement means the same everywhere and ensures fairness in trade.
s: The confusion or unfairness it causes

questions.q:
A cargo flight needs 6,400 kg of fuel. The fuel's density is 0.80 kg per litre, which is 1.76 lb per litre.
(i) How many litres are needed?
(ii) A crew member divides 6,400 by 1.76. How many litres does the plane get?
(iii) By how many litres is it short?
(iv) What percentage of the fuel needed was loaded?
(v) Which single step of working would have prevented the error?
questions.a: (i) 6400/0.80 = 8,000 L. (ii) 6400/1.76 = about 3,636 L. (iii) 8000 - 3636 = about 4,364 L short. (iv) 3636/8000 = about 45.5%. (v) Keeping to SI units, kilograms per litre, throughout.

questions.q: Justify, using the kilogram, the symbol c and the fuel story, why science depends on a shared language of terms, symbols and units. Finish by saying which of the three examples shows the cost of ignoring it most clearly.
questions.a: The kilogram rests on an agreed international standard, so results can be compared and trade is fair. The symbol c comes from history and international agreement, so everyone means the same constant. Together terms, symbols and units let scientists describe observations, compare results and build ideas together. In the fuel story, mixing pounds and kilograms left the plane about 15,000 litres short, so that example shows the cost most clearly.
s: Kilogram: agreed standard, comparison and fairness
Links to describing, comparing and building ideas
Names the fuel story with a reason

questions.q:
A school in Kochi receives a lab kit from abroad. Its booklet gives the density of a liquid as 2.2 lb per litre, but the school's balances read in kilograms. Take 1 kg as about 2.2 lb. A student must find the mass of 3.5 litres of the liquid.
(a) What is the density in kilograms per litre?
(b) What mass does a student get if she uses the booklet's number as if it were kg per litre?
(c) By what percentage is her mass too high, and which story in the chapter does this repeat?
(d) The school can rewrite all 24 booklet pages in SI units (about a week of staff time) or leave the booklet as it is and put a warning on the cover. Choose one and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) 2.2/2.2 = 1.0 kg per litre. (b) 3.5 x 2.2 = 7.7 kg, instead of 3.5 kg. (c) (7.7 - 3.5)/3.5 = 120% too high; it repeats the airplane fuel story, where pounds per litre was used for kilograms per litre. (d) Either choice if justified: rewriting costs a week but removes the risk at source; the warning is quick but relies on each student remembering to convert.
s: Part (c): 120 per cent and the fuel story
Part (d): a justified choice with the cost named

questions.q:
At a weekly market in Raipur, a rice seller measures with a stone he calls '1 kg' that his father used. Inspectors find it weighs only 0.92 of a standard kilogram. A customer who pays for 5 'kg' of rice at Rs 60 per standard kilogram actually gets 4.6 kg. About 200 customers buy 5 'kg' from him each week.
(a) Using the chapter, why can customers complain that the stone is not a kilogram?
(b) How much money does one customer lose on a 5 'kg' purchase?
(c) What is the weekly loss to the customers together?
(d) The seller says customers trust him and a certified set of weights will cost him Rs 3,000. The market committee must decide whether to require certified weights. Give one point for and one against, then decide.
questions.a: (a) A kilogram rests on an agreed international standard, not on a local object or opinion, and a family stone is a local object. (b) The shortfall is 5 - 4.6 = 0.4 kg, so 0.4 x 60 = Rs 24. (c) 24 x 200 = Rs 4,800 a week. (d) For: certified weights ensure fairness in trade and the weekly loss is Rs 4,800. Against: Rs 3,000 is a cost to him and his customers' trust is real. A justified decision, naturally favouring the standard on fairness grounds, earns the mark.
s: Part (d): a point each way and a justified decision

questions.q: Meera must find where a toy car moving at a steady 0.5 m/s will be, 8 s after it leaves a start line. Following the chapter's order of thinking, what should she do first?
questions.a: Identify what is happening and the quantities, such as distance, time and velocity
o: Identify what is happening and the quantities, such as distance, time and velocity
Pick the equation that looks most familiar and put the numbers straight in at once
Guess a distance and check whether it sounds sensible for a toy car
Memorise every equation of motion before attempting any problem at all

questions.q: A fish farm in Andhra Pradesh counts its fish every month and wants to reason about next month's count. Which description matches the chapter's use of mathematics?
questions.a: An expression for the pattern of population growth, used to reason about the next count
o: An expression for the pattern of population growth, used to reason about the next count
A formula that makes counting the fish unnecessary, because maths replaces all observation
A table of the colours of the fish, since mathematics describes only appearances
A statement that a population cannot be described by any mathematical expression

questions.q: Kabir finds equations a hurdle and decides to memorise as many as he can. Which advice from the chapter suits him best?
questions.a: Understand the situation and its quantities first, so equations become guides
o: Understand the situation and its quantities first, so equations become guides
Memorise even more equations, since equations are only calculation tools
Avoid mathematics in science, since it is a hurdle and not a language
Skip the situation and read only the final form of each equation

questions.q: Asked where a train moving steadily at 90 km/h will be after 2 hours, Isha says, '90 km each hour, for 2 hours, so 180 km from the start.' Tarun writes a memorised formula but cannot say what its letters mean. Whose approach is closer to the chapter, and why?
questions.a: Isha's, because she reasons from what the quantities mean in the situation
o: Isha's, because she reasons from what the quantities mean in the situation
Tarun's, because he used a formula and a formula always gives a right answer
Both equally, because both can reach the same number in the end
Neither, because a train's position cannot be described mathematically

questions.q:
Match each study (column I) with the kind of mathematical description the chapter names for it (column II).
Column I: 1. A scientist predicts where a bus will be 30 minutes after it leaves the stand  2. A scientist studies how fast a substance is used up when two chemicals are mixed  3. A forester studies how the number of deer in a forest rises over the years  4. An engineer follows how the energy in a swinging system changes from one form to another
Column II: a. Rates of chemical reactions  b. Patterns of population growth  c. Changes in energy within a system  d. Motion using distance, time and velocity
questions.a: The bus is a motion question (distance, time, velocity), the chemicals are a reaction-rate question, the deer are population growth and the swing is a change of energy.

questions.q:
Read these statements about mathematics in science.
Statement 1: Mathematical expressions can describe changes in energy within a system.
Statement 2: To use mathematics in science, a student must first memorise the equations.
Statement 3: Once an equation is memorised, there is no need to identify the quantities in the situation.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 1 is correct. The chapter says using mathematics does not mean memorising equations; it means understanding the situation and identifying the relevant quantities first.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An equation is a compact statement about how certain quantities are related.
Reason (R): Mathematics in science is meant to be a hurdle that a student clears by memorising equations.
questions.a: A is true, as the chapter describes an equation. R is false: the chapter says mathematics is not meant to be a hurdle but a language that helps us think clearly.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A cyclist moves at a steady 18 km/h for 40 minutes. Using distance, time and velocity, she covers ___ km.
Which of these would the chapter NOT count as using mathematics as a language for thinking?
questions.a: The chapter says mathematics is for thinking, not only for finding numerical answers; substituting without understanding skips the thinking.
o: Substituting numbers into a remembered equation without asking what its quantities mean
Choosing the quantities that matter in a pond-population problem before writing any relation
Using distance, time and velocity to say where a car will be at a later moment
Using a relationship to reason about how the energy of a system changes

questions.q: True or False? The chapter says a student who cannot recall an equation from memory cannot do science. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Learning to use mathematics in science does not mean memorising equations. It means understanding the situation, identifying the relevant quantities and then using relationships to reason carefully.

questions.q:
A toy car moves steadily at 0.5 m/s from a start line.
(a) How far from the line is it after 8 s?
(b) Using your answer to (a) to find the relation, how long does it take to be 10 m from the line?
questions.a: (a) 0.5 x 8 = 4 m. (b) The car covers 0.5 m each second, so 10 m takes 10/0.5 = 20 s.

questions.q:
A pond has 200 fish. A student models that the count rises each month by 10% of the current number.
(a) How many fish does the model give after 1 month?
(b) Using (a), how many after 2 months?
Explain what the chapter means by calling an equation 'a compact statement about how certain things are related', using the motion example.
questions.a: An equation packs a relationship into a short statement. For motion, it relates distance, time and velocity, which lets us say where an object will be at a later moment.
s: An equation states a relationship between quantities

questions.q: Compare two students: one memorises an equation of motion, the other first works out what is moving and which quantities matter. Say what each can do with a new problem.
questions.a: The student who only memorised may fail when the situation changes, since she does not know what the symbols stand for. The student who understood the situation can identify the quantities and reason with the relationship, so the equation acts as a guide.
s: Memorising alone: limited with a new problem
Understanding first: can identify quantities and reason

questions.q: A water tank is filling at a steady rate. Name two quantities you would identify and state in words one relationship between them.
questions.a: For example, the volume of water that has entered and the time passed: with a steady rate, the volume added is the rate multiplied by the time.

questions.q: Rohan says, 'An equation is more than a calculation tool; it states how things are related, so I should understand the situation before I use it.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says an equation is a compact statement about how certain things are related, and that using mathematics in science means understanding the situation first, identifying the relevant quantities, and then reasoning with relationships.
s: An equation states relations between quantities

questions.q: A student works out that a bus moving at 20 km/h travels '100 km' in 5 minutes. Without using a formula for the right answer, show that the answer cannot be right.
questions.a: 100 km in 5 minutes (5/60 h) would need a speed of 100 / (5/60) = 1,200 km/h, far more than 20 km/h. In 5 minutes, the bus covers only 20 x 5/60 = about 1.7 km. Understanding the situation shows the answer is impossible.

questions.q: The chapter mentions chemical reaction rates, population growth and energy changes. Explain what idea these three have in common as uses of mathematics.
questions.a: Each is a situation in which some quantities change or are related, and a mathematical expression states that relationship clearly so it can be tested carefully. In each, the situation and the quantities are identified first and then relationships are used to reason.
s: Quantities that are related or change
Expression states the relationship so it can be tested

questions.q:
A train leaves a station at 9:00 am and moves steadily at 72 km/h.
(i) How far has it gone at 9:40 am?
(ii) A station lies 150 km from the start. How long does the train take to reach it?
(iii) At what clock time does it arrive?
(iv) Name the three quantities you used and say which one you found each time.
questions.a: (i) 72 x 40/60 = 48 km. (ii) 150/72 = about 2.083 h = 125 minutes = 2 h 5 min. (iii) 9:00 + 2 h 5 min = 11:05 am. (iv) Distance, time and velocity: in (i) distance was found; in (ii) time was found, with velocity known.
s: States which quantity was found in each part

questions.q: Justify the chapter's claim that 'mathematics becomes a powerful language for thinking, not just for finding numerical answers.' Use at least two of its examples (motion, reaction rates, population growth, energy change) and state the order of thinking it advises.
questions.a: Motion: distance, time and velocity let us reason about where an object will be later, not only compute a number. Population growth: an expression for the pattern lets us reason about how the count will change. The chapter advises understanding the situation first, then identifying the relevant quantities, then using mathematical relationships to reason. This makes equations helpful guides and not obstacles.
s: First example with what it lets us reason about
Second example with what it lets us reason about
Contrast with finding only a numerical answer

questions.q:
A fish farm in Kakinada starts with 500 fish and the owner records that the count rises each month by 12% of the current number. He must order extra feed before the count passes 700 fish. A bulk feed order costs Rs 40,000 if placed after the count reaches 600, and Rs 46,000 as an urgent order if placed later.
(a) Which quantities must the owner identify before writing any relation?
(b) How many fish does the model give after 2 months?
(c) After how many whole months does the model first pass 700?
(d) The model assumes a constant 12% growth. The owner can place the bulk order after month 2 or wait for a real count at month 3. Choose one and justify, using the chapter's idea of what a prediction is.
questions.a: (a) The starting number, the monthly rate of increase and the time in months. (b) 500 x 1.12 x 1.12 = 627.2, about 627 fish. (c) After 3 months the count is about 702, the first time above 700. (d) Either choice if justified: ordering after month 2 saves Rs 6,000 and acts on a reasoned expectation, but the model assumes a constant 12%; waiting uses a real count but may cost the urgent price.
s: Part (d): a justified choice that weighs Rs 6,000 against the model's assumption

questions.q:
A school bus leaves school at 3:30 pm and moves steadily at 30 km/h towards the stop where Anaya gets off, 12 km away. Her mother leaves home at 3:45 pm on a scooter at a steady 24 km/h and the stop is 4 km from her home.
(a) At what time does the bus reach the stop?
(b) At what time does her mother reach the stop?
(c) How long does Anaya wait before her mother arrives?
(d) The stop is beside a busy road. Her mother can leave at 3:45 pm as planned or at 3:40 pm. Choose one, naming a limit of the steady-speed model in your reasoning.
questions.a: (a) 12/30 h = 24 minutes, so 3:54 pm. (b) 4/24 h = 10 minutes, so 3:55 pm. (c) Anaya waits 1 minute. (d) Either choice if justified: leaving at 3:40 pm means she arrives first, at 3:50 pm, and is not left on the busy road, but she waits 4 minutes; the steady-speed model ignores traffic and stops, so the real times may differ, and leaving earlier gives a margin.
s: Part (d): a justified choice naming a limit of the model

questions.q: Dev notices that every time his school bus brakes hard, the students standing in it lurch forward. He writes this down as something that happens again and again. In the chapter's words, what has he recorded?
questions.a: A regular pattern, which is what a law describes
o: A regular pattern, which is what a law describes
An explanation of why it happens, which is what a theory gives
A broad idea applied to one case, which is what a principle is
An untested idea, which is what the word theory means in science

questions.q: A teacher says the atomic theory explains how molecules are formed. A student replies, 'Then it is only a guess.' Which response fits the chapter?
questions.a: A theory rests on careful testing and critical examination, so it is not a guess
o: A theory rests on careful testing and critical examination, so it is not a guess
A theory is a guess that becomes a law as soon as enough people accept it
The atomic theory cannot be tested, so the student has a fair point
Theory is simply another name for a law, so the two words never differ

questions.q: Hema climbs three floors by stairs and explains her tiredness by saying the energy she spends is accounted for by the height she gains. In the chapter's vocabulary, the idea she applies is a
questions.a: principle, a broad idea that makes sense of a given situation
o: principle, a broad idea that makes sense of a given situation
law, because it states a pattern seen at every school building
theory, because it explains why molecules form from atoms
model, because it reduces the climber to a single point

questions.q: A student writes: 'Newton's laws of motion explain the jerk of a stopping bus, and the atomic theory explains how molecules form.' How does the second go a step beyond the first?
questions.a: It explains why the patterns occur, using evidence gathered over time
o: It explains why the patterns occur, using evidence gathered over time
It describes the pattern more briefly than a law does in words
It applies the broad idea of conserved energy to one situation
It repeats the law with a mathematical relationship added to it

questions.q: Sana says the principle of conservation of energy and Newton's laws of motion are the same kind of statement. Which remark is most accurate by the chapter's wording?
questions.a: A law describes a regular pattern; a principle is a broad idea for a given situation
o: A law describes a regular pattern; a principle is a broad idea for a given situation
She is right, since both only describe a pattern in the same way as each other does
A principle explains why a pattern occurs, while a law is only a guess
A law applies only in physics, while a principle applies only in biology

questions.q:
Read these statements about laws and theories.
Statement 1: A law usually describes a regular pattern observed in nature, sometimes using mathematical relationships.
Statement 2: A theory explains why patterns occur, usually based on evidence gathered over time.
Statement 3: In science, a theory is an untested idea that becomes a principle once it is approved.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A theory in science is not an untested idea; it is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3
2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In science, a theory is an untested guess.
Reason (R): Scientific theories are always open to improvement and often change as new evidence becomes available.
questions.a: A is false: a theory is an explanation based on careful testing. R is true: openness to improvement is a key feature of science.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Ice cubes floated in water in 25 out of 25 trials. A tested explanation of why they float, built from evidence gathered over time, would be called a ___ in the chapter's sense.
questions.a: theory

questions.q: Which pairing of example and term does the chapter NOT make?
questions.a: The chapter uses Newton's laws of motion for the jerk in a stopping bus, and the atomic theory for how molecules are formed.
o: The atomic theory, used for the jerk felt when a bus stops
Newton's laws of motion, used for the jerk felt when a bus stops
The atomic theory, used for how molecules are formed
Conservation of energy, used for climbing up the stairs

questions.q: True or False? When new evidence does not fit a scientific theory, the theory may be improved, and this openness is what makes science reliable. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says theories are always open to improvement and often change as new evidence becomes available, which is a key feature that makes science reliable.

questions.q:
A teacher writes three lines:
X: 'Passengers jerk forward whenever a bus stops suddenly.'
Y: 'Atoms combine to form molecules, as evidence gathered over years shows.'
Z: 'The energy a climber spends is accounted for by the height she gains.'
(a) Name the best term (law, theory or principle) for each line.
(b) Which one goes a step further than describing a pattern?
questions.a: (a) X is a law, Y is a theory and Z is a principle. (b) Y, the theory, because it explains how molecules form instead of only describing a pattern.
s: Part (a): law, theory, principle correctly assigned
Part (b): the theory, because it explains why

questions.q:
Students agree that 'a dropped ball always falls to the ground' describes a regular pattern.
(a) Which of the chapter's terms best fits that statement?
(b) What more would a statement need to be called a theory about it?
questions.a: (a) A law, because it describes a regular pattern. (b) It would have to explain why the ball falls, based on evidence gathered over time.

questions.q: Differentiate between 'I have a theory about who ate my lunch' and the use of 'theory' in the chapter.
questions.a: In everyday talk, 'theory' can mean a guess or untested idea. In the chapter, a theory is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination, open to improvement as new evidence arrives.
s: Scientific sense: tested explanation open to improvement

questions.q: Complete these two sentences with your own example: 'A pattern I could describe as a law is ___.' 'A theory about it would have to add ___.'
questions.a: For example: 'a stone thrown up always comes back down' and 'an explanation of why it does, based on evidence'. Any pattern from daily life with a theory that explains why, supported by evidence, earns the marks.
s: A regular pattern from daily life
A theory adds an explanation of why, based on evidence

questions.q: A headline says, 'Scientists change a theory: science is not reliable!' Give a two-sentence reply using the chapter.
questions.a: A theory is an explanation based on testing and is always open to improvement as new evidence arrives. This openness to correction is a key feature that makes science reliable, so a revised theory shows science working, not failing.
s: Theories are open to change on evidence

questions.q: Imran says, 'A theory is a guess waiting to be proved, and once proved it becomes a law.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. In the chapter a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination. A law and a theory also do different jobs: a law describes a regular pattern, and a theory explains why it occurs. The chapter does not say a theory turns into a law.
s: A theory is a tested explanation, not a guess
Law describes, theory explains: different jobs

questions.q: A student writes, 'Newton's laws of motion explain how molecules are formed.' Using the chapter, show that this line cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter uses Newton's laws of motion to explain the jerk felt when a bus stops suddenly, which is a matter of motion. How molecules are formed is explained by the atomic theory. So the line gives the explanation of one example to a different one.
s: What Newton's laws are used for
Concludes the line mixes the two

questions.q: Write a situation from daily life (not climbing stairs) in which the principle of conservation of energy could be applied. Say what the principle helps make sense of there.
questions.a: For example, a child on a swing rising and falling: the principle of conservation of energy helps make sense of how the energy changes form as she moves. Any sensible situation with the principle linked to what it explains earns the marks.
s: What it helps make sense of

questions.q: Compare a law, a theory and a principle as the chapter describes them. For each, give what it does and the chapter's example, and then say which of the three a student is most likely to confuse with an everyday meaning, and why.
questions.a: A law describes a regular pattern, for example Newton's laws of motion and the jerk when a bus stops. A theory explains why patterns occur, based on evidence gathered over time, for example the atomic theory and how molecules form. A principle is a broad idea that helps make sense of a given situation, for example conservation of energy when climbing stairs. A student most often confuses 'theory' with a guess, but in science it is a tested explanation.
s: Names theory as the likely confusion
Explains it is not a guess

questions.q: A newspaper writes: 'Scientists once believed a theory, now they have changed it, so you cannot trust science.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter. Say what a theory is, why it can change, what the change shows, and give your overall judgement.
questions.a: A theory is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination, not a guess. It is open to improvement and often changes as new evidence becomes available. Such a change shows science correcting itself on evidence, which is a key feature that makes it reliable. The newspaper's conclusion is therefore not supported; the judgement is that revisions strengthen trust in science.
s: Why it can change: new evidence
A clear judgement on the newspaper's claim

questions.q:
At a wall-chart competition in a Jaipur school, three entries carry labels written by students. Entry A is labelled 'Theory': 'Newton's laws of motion: passengers jerk forward when a bus stops suddenly.' Entry B is labelled 'Law': 'The atomic theory: how molecules are formed.' Entry C is labelled 'Principle': 'Conservation of energy applied to climbing stairs.' The judges can disqualify wrongly labelled entries or ask the students to fix their labels and keep the marks for their explanations.
(a) Which labels are wrong, and what should each be?
(b) What does each wrong label get wrong about the job of its term?
(c) Why is the label on Entry C right?
(d) Choose between disqualifying the wrong entries and asking for corrections, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Entry A should be Law and Entry B should be Theory. (b) A law describes a regular pattern, which the bus jerk is; a theory explains why patterns occur, which the atomic theory does for molecules. (c) A principle is a broad idea that helps make sense of a given situation, and conservation of energy does that for climbing stairs. (d) Either choice if justified: disqualifying is strict on accuracy; asking for corrections keeps the students' correct explanations while the labels are fixed.
s: Part (a): A is a law and B is a theory
Part (b): the job of law versus theory
Part (c): principle as a broad idea for a situation

questions.q:
The Class 9 section of a school in Bhopal records, over 20 school days, whether the bus arrived late. There were 8 rainy days and 12 dry days; the bus was late on 7 of the rainy days and on 3 of the dry days. A student announces, 'My theory is that rain makes the bus late.' The principal is considering starting school 20 minutes later on rainy days.
(a) Is the student's statement of the pattern a law, a theory or something else in the chapter's sense?
(b) What percentage of rainy days and of dry days was the bus late?
(c) What would the student need before her idea could be called a theory in the chapter's sense?
(d) Should the principal change the start time on rainy days now or wait for a term of data? Justify.
questions.a: (a) It is a regular pattern found in the records, so it is law-like; it is not yet a theory because it does not explain why. (b) 7/8 = 87.5% of rainy days and 3/12 = 25% of dry days. (c) An explanation of why rain delays the bus, based on careful testing and evidence gathered over time. (d) Either choice if justified: acting now uses a strong pattern (87.5% against 25%) but on only 20 days; waiting gives a more evidence-based explanation but children are late meanwhile.
s: Part (a): a pattern, not yet a theory
Part (c): needs a tested explanation of why
Part (d): a justified decision weighing the evidence

questions.q: Rahul says, 'It will rain this afternoon because the clouds look dark.' Which follow-up question best makes his prediction scientifically testable, by the chapter's example?
questions.a: What is today's humidity, and was it above 80 per cent the last time it rained?
o: What is today's humidity, and was it above 80 per cent the last time it rained?
Will it rain this afternoon, yes or no, in your own honest opinion at this very moment today?
Do the clouds also look dark to your friends who live nearby this week?
Did someone you know post on social media that it would rain?

questions.q: A forecaster is accurate for the next six hours but unsure about ten days ahead. Which explanation matches the chapter?
questions.a: Tiny differences in temperature, pressure, humidity and wind can grow over time
o: Tiny differences in temperature, pressure, humidity and wind can grow over time
Forecasters only record the weather for the first few hours of each day
Natural laws stop applying once the forecast goes beyond a single day
Humidity and wind cannot be measured at all beyond six hours from now

questions.q: A school team's model predicts that a kicked football will land 30 m away, but it lands 24 m away. What should the team do first, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Re-examine their assumptions, model and measurements
o: Re-examine their assumptions, model and measurements
Reject the laws of motion, since the football did not obey them
Ignore the result, as predictions are never meant to be checked
Adjust the measured distance so it agrees with the predicted 30 m

questions.q: A forwarded message says food cooked during an eclipse becomes harmful. Which question follows the chapter's way of testing the claim?
questions.a: Does any physical, chemical or biological change happen to food during an eclipse?
o: Does any physical, chemical or biological change happen to food during an eclipse?
How many people have forwarded the message to their families and friends already today?
Which famous person was the first to post the message about it?
Does the message sound alarming enough for the claim to be true?

questions.q: Years later, more precise measurements show that a well-liked theory gives slightly wrong values under extreme conditions. Which reading fits the chapter?
questions.a: Such a failure is not a weakness; it is science's greatest strength, as evidence decides
o: Such a failure is not a weakness; it is science's greatest strength, as evidence decides
It proves that all of science is unreliable and should not be trusted by anyone at all
The new measurements should be dropped in order to protect the old theory
The theory was only an opinion from the beginning and never had any support

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the idea from the chapter it shows (column II).
Column I: 1. A teacher asks for today's humidity before accepting a rain claim  2. A forecast for two weeks away is less certain than one for tomorrow  3. A model-based football landing agrees with the kick  4. A ball lands elsewhere and the team rechecks its measurements
Column II: a. Very tiny differences in conditions can grow over time  b. Confidence in the underlying science grows  c. Scientists re-examine assumptions, models or measurements  d. Looking for measurable evidence and past patterns
questions.a: Asking for humidity looks for measurable evidence; the longer forecast suffers as tiny differences grow; a matching prediction raises confidence; a mismatch leads to re-examining assumptions, models or measurements.

questions.q:
Read these statements about prediction.
Statement 1: When predictions match observations, confidence in the underlying science grows.
Statement 2: A scientific prediction is a guess made before an experiment is done.
Statement 3: No scientific theory is ever final, and none is beyond question.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Predictions are reasoned expectations based on evidence and careful thinking, not guesses.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Weather forecasts are usually reliable for a few hours or days but less certain further into the future.
Reason (R): Very tiny differences in conditions such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind can grow over time and lead to something completely different.
questions.a: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: small differences grow as time passes, which makes distant forecasts less certain.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A forecaster's ten-day prediction is less reliable than her ten-hour one because very tiny differences in conditions ___ over time.
questions.a: grow

questions.q: True or False? If a scientific prediction does not match what is observed, scientists should at once reject the underlying theory. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. They first re-examine their assumptions, models or measurements; ideas are rejected on evidence, not on opinion or belief.

questions.q:
Varsha says it will rain because the clouds look dark.
(a) Name two measurable quantities Meghna could ask about to test this.
(b) Why is a plain yes/no impression such as 'clouds look dark' less useful?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: humidity, wind speed and direction, temperature (and whether it is dropping). (b) Yes/no impressions give no measurable data or past patterns to compare, which testable questions need.
s: Part (b): no measurable data or past patterns

questions.q:
On five past rainy days the humidity was 82, 85, 78, 90 and 84 per cent.
(a) On how many of the five days was it above 80 per cent?
(b) Using (a), give the percentage and say whether 'above 80 per cent' is a certain sign of rain.
questions.a: (a) Four days (82, 85, 90, 84). (b) 4/5 = 80%. A pattern that held on most but not all of the rainy days is useful evidence, but is not certain.
s: Part (b): 80 per cent and why it is not certain

questions.q: Compare 'the clouds look dark' with 'humidity is 84 per cent, wind is rising from the west and the temperature is dropping' as bases for predicting rain.
questions.a: The first is an impression with a yes/no answer; the second gives measurable data that can be compared with past patterns, so it is the more scientifically testable basis.
s: Second: measurable, comparable with past patterns

questions.q: Make a prediction about how your breathing will change when you climb three flights of stairs. Say how you would check it.
questions.a: Prediction: breathing becomes faster and deeper. Check: count breaths in one minute at rest and just after climbing and compare.

questions.q: A forecast of heavy rain three days ahead does not come true, and a friend says forecasting is useless. Reply using the chapter.
questions.a: Forecasts use measurements and models, and are usually reliable for a few hours or days but less certain further ahead because tiny differences grow. A miss is a reason to re-examine assumptions and models, not to call forecasting useless.
s: A miss leads to re-examination, not rejection

questions.q: Harsh says, 'A scientific prediction is a reasoned expectation, so when it fails the scientist throws away the idea behind it.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: predictions are reasoned expectations based on evidence. The second is wrong: when a prediction fails, scientists re-examine their assumptions, models or measurements, and reject ideas only on evidence, not on opinion.

questions.q: Anil says, 'Scientists give up an idea when it becomes unpopular or goes against belief.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The chapter says scientists do not reject ideas based on opinion or belief, but only on evidence. When predictions fail to match observations they re-examine assumptions, models or measurements, and no theory is beyond question.

questions.q: A message claims food is harmful during an eclipse because an eclipse is 'a play of shadows'. Using the chapter's questions, show that no mechanism supports this claim.
questions.a: An eclipse is just a play of shadows; asking what physical change occurs shows no significant temperature change is expected, and food left in an ordinary shadow does not go bad. So there is no physical, chemical or biological mechanism for the harm.
s: Checks temperature and food in shadow
No physical, chemical or biological mechanism

questions.q:
On ten rainy days the morning humidity readings (per cent) were 84, 79, 91, 88, 82, 76, 90, 85, 81 and 87.
(i) On how many days was it above 80 per cent?
(ii) What percentage of the days is that?
(iii) What is the mean reading?
(iv) Today it is 83 per cent. Why is a prediction of rain a reasoned expectation and not a guess?
(v) Name one more measurement you would ask for, and why.
questions.a: (i) Eight days. (ii) 8/10 = 80%. (iii) 843/10 = 84.3 per cent. (iv) It rests on measured evidence and a past pattern: most past rainy days had humidity above 80 per cent. (v) For example wind speed and direction, or whether temperature is dropping, because the chapter lists these as further measurable data.
s: Reasoned expectation from evidence and pattern
A further measurable quantity with a reason

questions.q: Evaluate the chapter's statement that the failure of a prediction or a theory under new conditions is 'not a weakness of science' but 'its greatest strength'. Use the football example, the weather forecast and the way theories change, and end with a judgement.
questions.a: When the football lands elsewhere, the team re-examines its assumptions, model and measurements, so the mismatch drives deeper understanding. Forecasts fail when tiny differences grow, which shows where a model has limits. Theories may fail when new conditions are explored or measurements become more precise; scientists then revise them on evidence and not opinion. No theory is final, so being corrected by nature is what lets science explain the world. Judgement: the statement is justified.
s: Forecast failure shows limits of a model
Theories revised on evidence, not opinion

questions.q:
A school weather club in Chennai records the morning humidity (per cent) and whether it rained that afternoon on 12 days. Humidity and rain (R) or no rain (N): 84 R, 78 N, 91 R, 82 N, 88 R, 70 N, 86 R, 79 N, 90 R, 83 R, 75 N, 81 N. Their rule is: 'predict rain if the morning humidity is above 80 per cent'. The school wants to use the rule at 8 am to decide whether to cancel an afternoon sports event.
(a) Why is this rule a better basis for a prediction than 'the clouds look dark'?
(b) On how many of the 12 days was the rule correct, and what percentage is that?
(c) On how many days that the rule flagged rain did it not rain, and what does the chapter say to do about these misses?
(d) Should the school cancel on the rule's word at 8 am, or wait till noon and check wind and temperature too? Justify.
questions.a: (a) It uses a measurable quantity and past data, not an impression. (b) The rule flagged 8 days and rained on 6; the 4 days at or below 80 per cent were all dry. Correct days are 6 + 4 = 10 of 12, which is 83.3%. (c) It did not rain on 2 of the 8 flagged days (82 and 81 per cent); the chapter says to re-examine the assumptions, model and measurements, for example by adding wind and temperature. (d) Either choice if justified: cancelling at 8 am gives early notice but 2 in 8 flagged days (25%) would be wrong; waiting for more measurements improves reliability but leaves less time to plan.
s: Part (d): a justified choice with the 25 per cent false-alarm figure

questions.q:
During a solar eclipse, the Class 9 science club of a school near Kolkata tests the claim 'food becomes harmful during an eclipse'. They keep two identical bowls of cooked rice, one in the open during the eclipse and one in the open at the same hour on the next day. The air temperature at the start of the eclipse is 33.0 degrees Celsius and at its peak is 32.4 degrees Celsius. Both bowls begin to smell sour at about the same time, after nine hours.
(a) Which two of the chapter's questions does this test address?
(b) By how many degrees, and by what percentage of 33.0, did the temperature fall at the peak?
(c) What do the two bowls suggest about the claim?
(d) The school can send a note saying 'eating during an eclipse is safe' or only publish the results and let families decide. Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) Does temperature change significantly during an eclipse, and does food go bad if left in a shadow. (b) 33.0 - 32.4 = 0.6 degrees, which is about 1.8% of 33.0. (c) Both bowls turned sour at about the same time, so the eclipse made no difference, which fits the chapter's finding that no physical, chemical or biological mechanism supports the claim. (d) Either choice if justified: the note gives a clear message based on evidence; publishing only the results respects families' beliefs but may leave the claim unchallenged.
s: Part (c): no mechanism, the bowls turn sour together

questions.q: Rohit counts 14 breaths a minute at rest. Taking 1440 minutes in a day, about how many breaths does he take in a day, to the nearest thousand?
questions.a: 14 x 1440 = 20,160, which is about 20,000 breaths.
o: About 20,000
About 2,000
About 200,000
About 10,000

questions.q: Ananya finds that a 2-litre party balloon fills in 5 breaths. About how much air is in one breath?
questions.a: 2 litres / 5 breaths = 0.4 litre per breath.
o: About 0.4 litre
About 10 litres
About 2.5 litres
About 0.04 litre

questions.q: One student estimates that a family of four needs 100 g of rice for a whole month; another gets 4 tonnes. Which comment fits the chapter?
questions.a: Both answers are unreasonable: 100 g is far too little and several tonnes is far too much
o: Both answers are unreasonable: 100 g is far too little and several tonnes is far too much
100 g is reasonable, because rice is a light food and one month is quite a short period of time
Only the 4 tonnes is unreasonable, since an answer that is too small is always safe
Neither can be judged without an exact value of the calories in rice

questions.q: After estimating about 10,000 litres of air breathed in a day, Dilip blows up balloons at 20 s each to get a second estimate. Why does the chapter suggest this?
questions.a: A second, independent method with a close value builds confidence in the first
o: A second, independent method with a close value builds confidence in the first
It replaces the first estimate with an exact value that is guaranteed to be correct
It shows that blowing up balloons is the same activity as normal breathing
It proves that the first estimate must have been wrong from the start

questions.q:
Match each calculation (column I) with its result (column II).
Column I: 1. 12 breaths a minute for 1440 minutes  2. A 2-litre balloon filled in 4 breaths, per breath  3. 3 balloons a minute, 2 litres each, for 1440 minutes  4. 20,000 breaths of 0.5 litre each
Column II: a. 0.5 litre  b. 17,280 breaths  c. 10,000 litres  d. 8,640 litres

Read these statements about estimation.
Statement 1: Exact values are not always necessary, especially in the early stages of reasoning.
Statement 2: Two independent rough methods that come out reasonably close build confidence in an estimate.
Statement 3: An approximate estimate can be enough to tell us whether a result is reasonable or impossible.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are supported: the chapter says estimates help to build intuition, detect errors and judge whether a result is reasonable or impossible.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Estimating the litres of air breathed in a day does not need an exact value.
Reason (R): There are 60 x 24 = 1440 minutes in a day.
questions.a: Both are true, but the number of minutes in a day does not explain why an estimate suffices; the aim is a reasonable estimate, not an exact one.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: An adult needs 2000 kcal a day. Assuming all calories come from rice, a family of four needs ___ kcal in a 30-day month.
Which statement about estimation would the chapter NOT support?
questions.a: The chapter says exact values are not always necessary and that careful reasoning is valued perhaps much more than accurate calculation.
o: An estimate is of no use unless it matches the exact value to three digits
An estimate can help to detect an error in a longer calculation
Careful reasoning matters more than an accurate calculation here
A rough answer can show that a result is reasonable or impossible

questions.q: True or False? Estimates of about 10,000 litres and 8,640 litres of air breathed per day, made by two different methods, are close enough for estimation purposes. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. 8,640 is about 86% of 10,000. The chapter calls them reasonably close for estimation purposes, and agreement between independent methods builds confidence.

questions.q:
Take 2,200 kcal per adult per day and 350 kcal in 100 g of cooked rice.
(a) How many kcal does a family of four need per day?
(b) Using (a), about how many grams of rice does the family need per day?

A person takes 13 breaths a minute at rest, and one breath is about 0.4 litre.
(a) How many breaths are taken in a day of 1440 minutes?
(b) Using (a), about how many litres of air is that?
Name two benefits of learning to estimate that the chapter mentions, and give one situation for either.
questions.a: It helps build intuition, detect errors and develop confidence. For example, estimating a family's monthly rice shows quickly that 100 g is too little or a few tonnes too much.

questions.q: The balloon cross-check assumes someone blows balloons without a break for a whole day. Does that make it useless? Answer with the chapter.
questions.a: No. It is an independent rough method used for estimation purposes, and it came out reasonably close. The chapter itself notes that we would tire quickly, unlike restful breathing, so it is a check, not a literal description.
s: It is a useful independent check
Its limit acknowledged, not a literal claim

questions.q: Choose the quantities you would use to estimate how many litres of water your family drinks in a week, and write the multiplication that gives the estimate.
questions.a: For example: number of people x glasses per person per day x litres per glass x 7 days. Any set of sensible, identified quantities with the multiplication earns the marks.

questions.q: Priya estimates that a family of four needs about 1 kg of rice for a whole month. 'Estimates need not be exact, so that is fine,' she says. Take 350 kcal in 100 g and 2,000 kcal per adult per day. Is she right?
questions.a: No. Needed energy is 4 x 2,000 x 30 = 240,000 kcal, and 240,000 / 350 x 100 = about 68,571 g, nearly 69 kg. An estimate need not be exact, but 1 kg is far too small, like the 100 g the chapter calls clearly too little.
s: Not exact is allowed, absurdly small is not

questions.q: Imran says, 'Two independent methods gave 10,000 and 8,640 litres a day, so the first estimate seems reasonable.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The two values come from independent methods and are reasonably close, about 86% of each other. The chapter says that for estimation purposes this builds confidence in the first estimate.
s: Values are reasonably close, building confidence

questions.q: A student claims a person breathes in 2,000,000 litres of air a day and takes about 20,000 breaths. Show that this cannot be right, using what the chapter says about a breath.
questions.a: 2,000,000 / 20,000 = 100 litres per breath. But about 4 to 5 breaths fill a 2-litre balloon, so one breath is about 0.4 to 0.5 litre. 100 litres per breath is hundreds of times too large, so the claim is impossible.
s: Compares with about 0.5 litre per breath

questions.q:
Estimate the rice a family of four needs for a month of 30 days. Take 2,250 kcal per adult per day, all from rice, and 350 kcal in 100 g of cooked rice.
(i) Daily kcal for the family.
(ii) Kcal for the month.
(iii) Mass of rice in kg for the month.
(iv) Is the answer neither absurdly small nor absurdly large? Use the chapter's limits.
(v) What range does the 2,000 to 2,500 kcal need give?
questions.a: (i) 4 x 2,250 = 9,000 kcal. (ii) 9,000 x 30 = 270,000 kcal. (iii) 270,000 / 350 x 100 = about 77,143 g, about 77 kg. (iv) 77 kg is far above 100 g and far below a few tonnes, so it is reasonable. (v) At 2,000 it is about 68.6 kg and at 2,500 about 85.7 kg, so roughly 69 to 86 kg.
s: Sanity check against 100 g and a few tonnes

questions.q: The chapter says science values careful reasoning perhaps much more than accurate calculations. Using the estimate of air breathed in a day, justify this. Cover the breaths per day, the volume of a breath, the first answer, the cross-check, and your judgement.
questions.a: At rest about 12 to 15 breaths a minute give about 20,000 breaths in 1440 minutes. About 4 to 5 breaths fill a 2-litre balloon, so one breath is about 0.5 litre. That gives about 10,000 litres a day. Filling about 3 balloons a minute gives 3 x 2 x 1440 = 8,640 litres, reasonably close. The aim was a reasonable estimate through careful steps, not an exact figure, so reasoning counted more than precise calculation.
s: About 20,000 breaths from 12 to 15 a minute
About 0.5 litre per breath from the balloon

questions.q:
Zoya, in a school in Shillong, estimates the air she breathes in a day. She counts 14 breaths a minute at rest. She finds that 5 breaths fill a 2-litre party balloon. As a cross-check, she times herself blowing up a balloon, which takes 25 s.
(a) How many litres of air per breath, and how many litres a day (1440 minutes) does the first method give?
(b) How many balloons a minute does she blow, and how many litres a day does the cross-check give?
(c) By what percentage is the cross-check lower than the first estimate?
(d) She can report 'about 8,000 litres' or the range '6,900 to 8,100 litres'. Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) 2/5 = 0.4 litre per breath; 14 x 1440 x 0.4 = 8,064 litres. (b) 60/25 = 2.4 balloons a minute; 2.4 x 2 x 1440 = 6,912 litres. (c) (8,064 - 6,912)/8,064 = about 14.3% lower. (d) Either choice if justified: the single figure is simple and fine for estimation, but the range is more honest about the gap between two rough methods.
s: Part (a): 0.4 litre per breath and 8,064 litres
Part (b): 2.4 balloons a minute and 6,912 litres

questions.q:
The mess of a hostel in Mysuru feeds 120 students. The cook wants to estimate the daily rice. Each student needs 2,200 kcal a day, 60% of it from rice, and 100 g of cooked rice gives 350 kcal. The cook has been ordering 30 kg of rice a day, at Rs 50 per kg.
(a) How many kcal per day must rice supply for all 120 students?
(b) About how many kg of rice does that need?
(c) What percentage of the need does 30 kg meet?
(d) The cook can order 45 kg or 50 kg a day. Choose one and justify, considering cost and the estimate's roughness.
questions.a: (a) 120 x 2,200 x 0.6 = 158,400 kcal. (b) 158,400 / 350 x 100 = about 45,257 g, about 45.3 kg. (c) 30 / 45.3 = about 66%. (d) Either choice if justified: 45 kg costs Rs 2,250 and fits the estimate; 50 kg costs Rs 2,500, Rs 250 more, giving a margin for the roughness of an estimate but risking waste.
s: Part (d): a justified choice with the Rs 250 difference

questions.q: A town wants to cut plastic waste. Its team has a chemist, a biologist, a mathematician and an artist. A councillor says only the chemist is needed, because plastic is a chemistry topic. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Real problems rarely stay in one branch; several disciplines are needed together
o: Real problems rarely stay in one branch; several disciplines are needed together
He is right, because each real-world problem belongs to exactly one branch of science
The artist is not needed, because science never connects with the arts
The mathematician is not needed, because mathematics lies outside science

questions.q: A team tests how well a mask filter stops particles by modelling how air flows through it. Which branch of the chapter's list does this belong to?
questions.a: Mathematics, modelling airflow and filtration efficiency
o: Mathematics, modelling airflow and filtration efficiency
Chemistry, studying the properties of polymer fibres
Biology, studying the size and behaviour of viruses
Physics, studying particle motion and electrostatic attraction

questions.q: Aarti says, 'The branches of science are lines drawn in nature itself, so physics never touches biology.' How does the chapter respond?
questions.a: The divisions are made by us to organise knowledge; nature has no such boundaries
o: The divisions are made by us to organise knowledge; nature has no such boundaries
She is right, since each branch studies a separate part of nature on its own
She is right, but only for Grades 9 and 10 and not after them
The branches are independent of each other, so each needs no other

questions.q: Ravi will not study science after Grade 10, and his sister says scientific thinking is then of no use to him. Which reasoning fits the chapter's last paragraphs?
questions.a: It helps him understand technology and judge information critically in any work
o: It helps him understand technology and judge information critically in any work
She is right, since scientific thinking is useful only to people who study science
She is right, because science is just a list of facts to memorise for exams
She is wrong, but only because every job demands a science certificate

questions.q: The chapter says science has grown through the work of many individuals across different cultures and generations. Which situation illustrates this best?
questions.a: A researcher shares results, others test them, and a mistake is corrected
o: A researcher shares results, others test them, and a mistake is corrected
A single scientist announces a final answer which nobody is allowed to question
A laboratory keeps its results private so that nobody can check its work
A textbook's facts are memorised by students and never examined again

questions.q:
Read these statements about the branches of science.
Statement 1: The natural world has clear boundaries that match the branches of science.
Statement 2: Developing medicines is a problem that only chemistry can solve.
Statement 3: Science connects naturally with mathematics, technology, arts and social sciences.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is correct. The branches are divisions made by us to organise knowledge, and most real problems, including developing medicines, need ideas from several disciplines.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Science is complete once a textbook states its facts, equations and experiments.
Reason (R): Science is a human activity that grows as people ask questions, test ideas, share results and learn from mistakes.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says science is not just a collection of facts, equations or experiments. R is true: it grows through questioning, testing, sharing and learning from mistakes.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: A team studies the properties of the polymer fibres in a mask filter. Of physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics, the chapter places this work under ___.
questions.a: chemistry

questions.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the chapter's closing paragraphs?
questions.a: The chapter says science is not just a collection of facts, equations or experiments; it is a human activity that keeps growing.
