o: Science is a finished collection of facts, equations and experiments
Science grows as people share results and learn from mistakes
Science is shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration and careful questioning
Scientific thinking helps people evaluate information critically

questions.q: True or False? The natural world is divided into physics, chemistry, biology and earth science, so a real-world problem belongs to exactly one of them. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The divisions are made by us only to organise knowledge; nature has no such boundaries, and problems such as climate change need ideas from several disciplines together.

questions.q:
A designer is studying a new mask fabric.
(a) Which branch, according to the chapter, would model airflow and filtration efficiency?
(b) Which branch would explain why tiny particles can be pulled onto the fibres by electrostatic attraction?
questions.a: (a) Mathematics. (b) Physics, which the chapter lists for particle motion and electrostatic attraction.

questions.q:
(a) Name two areas outside the branches of science with which the chapter says science connects naturally.
(b) Using one of them, say how it might help a school's campaign against air pollution.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: mathematics, technology, arts, social sciences. (b) For example, the arts can make posters that carry the message, or social sciences can study how people in the neighbourhood travel to school.

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'branch of science' and a 'boundary in nature', using the chapter.
questions.a: A branch such as physics or biology is a division made by us to help organise knowledge. A boundary in nature would be a real separation, but the chapter says the natural world has none and the branches are not independent of each other.
s: Branch: a human division to organise knowledge
No such boundary exists in nature

questions.q: Choose a bicycle helmet. Name two branches of science involved in it and one idea from each.
questions.a: For example, physics: how a soft lining spreads the force of an impact over time; chemistry: the properties of the foam and plastic used. Any two branches with a sensible idea each earn the marks.

questions.q: A student says that hiding a failed experiment makes her science look better. Respond using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says science grows as people ask questions, test ideas, share results and learn from mistakes, so sharing a failed attempt helps others and herself learn. Hiding it removes this.
s: Science grows by sharing results and learning from mistakes
Hiding a failure removes that learning

questions.q: Meena says, 'The chapter says the branches of science are divisions made by us and not boundaries in nature.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the natural world does not have such boundaries; the divisions are made by us only to help organise knowledge, and they are not independent of each other. Real problems such as climate change need ideas from several disciplines.
s: Divisions are made by us to organise knowledge

questions.q: Tarun says, 'I will not study science after Grade 10, so scientific thinking will not matter to me.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The chapter says scientific thinking will be very important in whatever he does: it helps him understand the technology around him, evaluate information critically and make sense of the world he lives in.
s: Helps evaluate information and make sense of the world

questions.q: Show that physics alone cannot fully explain how a mask works, using the chapter's list.
questions.a: The chapter says understanding a mask needs physics for particle motion and electrostatic attraction, but also chemistry for the properties of polymer fibres, biology for the size and behaviour of viruses, and mathematics for modelling airflow and filtration efficiency. Physics covers only one of the four needs.
s: Names what chemistry and biology add

questions.q: Use the mask example. For each of physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics, state what it contributes to understanding how a mask works. Then say what this example teaches about the branches of science.
questions.a: Physics: particle motion and electrostatic attraction. Chemistry: the properties of polymer fibres. Biology: the size and behaviour of viruses. Mathematics: modelling airflow and filtration efficiency. The example shows that a real problem does not stay inside one branch; the branches are human divisions, and solving problems needs them together.

questions.q: Justify the chapter's view that science 'is not just a collection of facts, equations, or experiments' but 'a human activity'. Mention the qualities that shape it, how it grows, who contributes, and why scientific thinking matters even to someone who does not study science further.
questions.a: The chapter says science is shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration and careful questioning. It grows as people ask questions, test ideas, share results and learn from mistakes. It develops through the work of many individuals across different cultures and generations. Scientific thinking helps anyone understand technology and evaluate information critically, so it matters beyond the classroom.
s: Growth through testing, sharing and mistakes
Many people across cultures and generations
A clear conclusion tied to the claim

questions.q:
A municipal committee in Surat must choose a mask fabric for 5,000 school children. A panel of a physicist, a chemist, a biologist and a mathematician reports. Fabric A filters 92% of test particles and lets air through at 60 litres a minute; it costs Rs 12 a mask. Fabric B filters 85% and lets air through at 90 litres a minute; it costs Rs 8 a mask.
(a) Which of the four experts' fields does each of the two fabric facts (filtering percentage and airflow) fall under, according to the chapter?
(b) How many percentage points more does A filter, how many times as much air does B pass, and what is the cost difference for 5,000 masks?
(c) Why can no one branch alone decide?
(d) Choose A or B and justify, saying what you give up.
questions.a: (a) Both the filtering percentage and the airflow are modelled by mathematics (airflow and filtration efficiency), with particle behaviour from physics and the fibres from chemistry. (b) 92 - 85 = 7 percentage points; 90/60 = 1.5 times; 5,000 x (12 - 8) = Rs 20,000. (c) The choice needs physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics together; the branches are divisions made by us, not boundaries. (d) Either choice if justified: A filters more but costs Rs 20,000 more and lets less air through; B costs less and passes 1.5 times the air but filters 7 points less.
s: Part (a): filtration efficiency and airflow are mathematics-modelled, with other branches
Part (d): a justified choice naming what is given up

questions.q:
A district science fair in Nashik has 40 projects. Twenty-two use ideas from one branch only (physics, chemistry or biology) and 18 combine two or more branches. A group from one school reports that its first water-purifier attempt failed, how it found the reason, and shares its data with another school, which then improves the design. The judges debate whether to give extra marks for combined-branch projects and for honest reporting of failures, or to score only the final result.
(a) What percentage of the projects combine branches?
(b) Which statement in the chapter supports giving credit to combined-branch projects?
(c) What does the chapter say about the failed attempt and its sharing?
(d) Should the judges give extra marks for honest reporting of failures or score only the final result? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 18/40 = 45%. (b) The natural world has no boundaries; the branches are divisions made by us, and real problems need several disciplines together. (c) Science grows as people ask questions, test ideas, share results and learn from mistakes, so the failed attempt and its sharing are part of how science works. (d) Either choice if justified: extra marks encourage honest reporting and collaboration; scoring only the final result is simpler and rewards the best working design.
s: Part (b): no boundaries; problems need several disciplines
Part (c): mistakes and sharing help science grow
